layers.name: subtitle
layers.text: what you see, and why it happens

children.name: label
children.text:
the corona: the sun's
outer atmosphere

children.name: label
children.text:
prominences: glowing
gas on the sun's edge

children.name: body
children.text:
The moon passes between us and the sun. Its lit side
faces away, so in the bright sky you cannot see it.

children.name: body
children.text:
The moon's edge touches the sun's. A small bite
appears, and it grows for more than an hour.

children.name: body
children.text:
The eye adapts: with the sun nine tenths covered the
day hardly looks darker, though most of its light is gone.

children.name: body
children.text:
The last sunlight shines through valleys on the moon's
edge, until one point is left: the diamond ring.

children.name: body
children.text:
The moon covers the whole sun. Its corona appears,
stars and planets come out, dusk glows all around.

children.name: body
children.text:
The sun is about 400 times wider than the moon and
about 400 times farther away: they look the same size.

children.name: body
children.text:
Sunlight bursts back as a diamond ring on the other
side. From here on, only look through eclipse glasses.

children.name: body
children.text:
The moon moves on. Its shadow races away over the
Earth at well over a thousand kilometres an hour.

children.name: body
children.text:
The moon leaves the sun. The same spot on Earth sees
a total eclipse only every few centuries.

layers.name: safety
layers.text: Never look at the sun without eclipse glasses, except during totality.
